title: LLM 推理的 Roofline 模型
author: Sachin Kr. Rajput
content:
In Part 3 the Word Factory had two speed limits. The forklift brings tables from the warehouse, and the workbench does the math. Reading your question got stuck on the workbench. Typing the answer got stuck on the forklift.

Today we draw both limits on one picture. Engineers call it the roofline model, and it's the most useful sketch I know for LLM inference. Once you have it, you can look at any chip, any model and any batch size and say which limit you'll hit, before you run anything.

The whole model fits in one line:

speed = the smaller of (workbench speed) and (forklift speed × math per byte)

Let's unpack that, measure it, and then use it.

One number per job: math per byte

Every job the factory does has a recipe: how many math steps (FLOPs) it needs, and how many bytes the forklift must bring for it. Divide one by the other and you get the job's math per byte. Engineers call it arithmetic intensity.

A few jobs from earlier parts:

  • One token through a big table. Each table number is 4 bytes and gets used for 2 FLOPs (one multiply, one add). That's 0.5 FLOPs per byte.
  • 256 tokens through the same table. The table is fetched once and used 256 times: about 122 FLOPs per byte.
  • Adding two lists of numbers. Fetch two numbers (8 bytes), write one (4 bytes), do 1 FLOP: about 0.08 FLOPs per byte.

Same factory, same tables, numbers that are 1,500 times apart. That spread is the whole story of LLM speed.

Drawing the roof

Now picture a chart. Left to right is math per byte. Bottom to top is speed (FLOPs per second).

The slanted roof is the forklift. If a job does 1 FLOP per byte and the forklift brings 15 billion bytes per second, the job can't go faster than 15 billion FLOPs per second, however fast the workbench is. Do 2 FLOPs per byte and the limit doubles. So this roof is a slope: forklift speed × math per byte.

The flat roof is the workbench. Past a certain point the forklift keeps up easily, and the workbench's top speed is the limit.

Where they meet is the ridge. It's the workbench speed divided by the forklift speed. Jobs to the left of the ridge are memory-bound. Jobs to the right are compute-bound.

In code, that's all of it: 

def roof(intensity):                 # FLOPs per byte -> best possible FLOPs per second
    return min(PEAK, BW * intensity)

I measured the two roofs the same way as in Part 3, with roofline.py: one token through a 400 MB table for the forklift, and a big multiply that fits near the workbench for the math: 

memory roof :   15.0 GB/s
math roof   :  164.3 GFLOP/s
ridge point :   11.0 FLOPs per byte

(The cloud CPU ran a little faster today than for Part 3, which measured 12 GB/s and 121 GFLOP/s. The ridge barely moved: 11 instead of 10. That's a hint for later.)

So on this computer, any job that does fewer than 11 FLOPs per byte is waiting on the forklift.

Putting real jobs under the roof

The roof is a prediction. Let's test it. The same script times three kinds of jobs, each one sized so it can't hide in the chip's cache: 

# 1) the model's tables: a 400 MB table, N tokens on the trip
for B in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512]:
    X = np.random.rand(N, B).astype(np.float32)
    sec = timed(lambda: W @ X)

# 2) typing for many users: each one reads their OWN 25 MB notebook
sec = timed(lambda: [k @ q for k, q in zip(K, Q)])

# 3) a small step: add two lists of 50 million numbers
sec = timed(lambda: np.add(u, v, out=out))

Each test ran several times and I kept the middle result: 

operation                      FLOP/B   GFLOP/s      roof of roof
table x 1 tokens                 0.50       7.7       7.5    103%
table x 2 tokens                 1.00       6.4      15.0     43%
table x 4 tokens                 2.00      14.2      29.9     47%
table x 8 tokens                 3.99      27.7      59.7     46%
table x 16 tokens                7.97      49.5     119.3     41%
table x 32 tokens               15.90      77.6     164.3     47%
table x 64 tokens               31.60     103.1     164.3     63%
table x 128 tokens              62.40     118.8     164.3     72%
table x 256 tokens             121.77     143.2     164.3     87%
table x 512 tokens             232.22     156.0     164.3     95%
notebook read, 16 users          0.50       6.9       7.5     92%
notebook read, 64 users          0.50       6.6       7.5     89%
add two lists                    0.08       0.8       1.2     66%

And here's the same thing as a picture:

Four things to notice.

1. More tokens walk you up the slope. One token sits at the bottom left, stuck on the forklift. Every time you double the tokens on the trip, the job moves right and climbs. Past the ridge it reaches the flat roof: at 512 tokens the table multiply ran at 95% of the workbench's top speed. (The 1-token row sits right on the roof because it's the same job I used to measure the forklift.)

2. The roof is a ceiling, not a promise. Between 2 and 16 tokens, the points sit at about half their roof. Nothing in the hardware forces that. The math library just uses a less efficient method for "skinny" multiplies with only a few tokens. Real GPU servers ship special code for exactly this small-batch zone, because that's where typing lives. When a job sits far below its roof, the roofline tells you there's speed left on the table, and roughly how much.

3. Notebooks don't walk. With 16 users or 64 users, reading notebooks stays at 0.5 FLOPs per byte. Batching moved the table jobs to the right, but it can't move these, because every user brings their own notebook and nothing is shared. This is Part 3's "the notebooks don't share", seen on the roofline. (Real models share each notebook between a few attention heads, a trick called grouped-query attention, which lifts this to a few FLOPs per byte. Still far left of the ridge.)

4. Small steps live in the basement. Adding two lists does 0.08 FLOPs per byte, the lowest point on the chart. That's why, in Part 2, the tiny steps between the big tables took far more time than their share of the math. It's also why real engines glue small steps together into one pass (kernel fusion): fewer trips for the forklift.

Where LLM inference lands

Put the pieces of an LLM on this chart and the two phases from Part 3 fall right out:

Job Math per byte Where it lands
Typing, 1 user, the model's tables ~0.5 (float32), ~1 (2-byte numbers) Far left. Forklift.
Typing, many users, the tables grows with the number of users Climbs the slope as the batch grows
Reading a 256-token question ~120 Right of the ridge. Workbench.
Typing, reading each user's notebook ~0.5 to a few, for any batch size Stuck on the left
Small steps (adds, norms) ~0.1 The basement

One handy shortcut: when the tables are stored as 2-byte numbers (BF16, how most models are served), every number does 2 FLOPs per token and costs 2 bytes. So math per byte ≈ the number of tokens on the trip. Want to know if a batch keeps the math busy? Compare the batch size with the ridge.

Predict before you run

Now the payoff. To draw a roofline for any chip you need just two numbers from its spec sheet: memory bandwidth and dense math speed.

  • NVIDIA H100 SXM: 3.35 TB/s and 989 TFLOP/s (BF16, without the "sparsity" bonus that some spec sheets add). Ridge: about 295 FLOPs per byte.
  • NVIDIA B200: 8 TB/s and 2,250 TFLOP/s (BF16, dense). Ridge: about 281.

That's a forklift about 220 times faster than my CPU's and a workbench about 6,000 times faster. The ridge is 27 times further right than my CPU's 11. On a big GPU the workbench is so fast that almost everything is waiting on memory.

Here's predict.py applying the one-line model to an 8-billion-parameter model in BF16 (16 GB of tables) on one H100, counting only the tables: 

an 8-billion-parameter model in BF16 (16 GB of weights) on one H100
  tokens  step ms  fetch ms  math ms  tokens/s  limit
       1     4.78      4.78     0.02       209  memory
       8     4.78      4.78     0.13     1,675  memory
      64     4.78      4.78     1.04    13,400  memory
     256     4.78      4.78     4.14    53,600  memory
     512     8.28      4.78     8.28    61,812  math
    1024    16.57      4.78    16.57    61,812  math

Read it like a chatbot company would:

  • One user can never get more than ~209 words per second from this model on this chip. The forklift needs 4.78 ms to bring 16 GB, and the math takes 0.02 ms of that. No amount of workbench helps.
  • Up to a few hundred users ride for free. From 1 to 256 tokens per trip, the step time doesn't change at all. Every extra user is pure profit, until you pass the ridge.
  • Past the ridge, the bill arrives. At 512 and 1,024 tokens per trip the step gets longer, because now you're waiting on the workbench.

And two predictions that surprise people: 

same model, 1 user, different number sizes on the H100
  BF16, 2 bytes   4.78 ms per token -> at most  209 tokens/s; ridge needs ~295 tokens per trip
  FP8, 1 byte     2.39 ms per token -> at most  419 tokens/s; ridge needs ~295 tokens per trip
  • Smaller numbers make one user type twice as fast. Storing the tables in 1-byte numbers (FP8) halves the bytes, so the forklift brings the whole model in half the time. That's why so much effort goes into quantization, the last part of this series.
  • But the ridge doesn't move. The chip also does FP8 math twice as fast, so you still need ~295 tokens per trip to keep the workbench busy. Newer chips are the same: the B200 raised both roofs, and the ridge stayed around 280 tokens.

How good is the prediction?

Remember, these are ceilings. Real engines land below them, and the notebooks add bytes the table-only math above ignores. Part 3 showed how fast that grows: at 64 users with 512 notes each, the notebooks were seven times bigger than the model. So real servers hit the forklift sooner and harder than this table says.

We can check the ceiling on our tiny factory, though. In Part 3, typing one word for one user meant fetching 377 MB (tables plus one notebook) with a forklift that, that day, did 12 GB/s. The roofline says that can't take less than 31 ms. The measurement was 37.5 ms, about 83% of the roof. One line of arithmetic, done before running anything, got within a fifth of the real answer.

How to use the roofline

  1. Find the two roofs. Memory bandwidth and dense math speed, from the spec sheet or a quick measurement.
  2. Find the ridge. Math speed ÷ bandwidth.
  3. Find your job's math per byte. For the model's tables with 2-byte numbers, it's about the number of tokens on the trip.
  4. Compare. Left of the ridge: you're paying for bytes, so fetch fewer (smaller numbers, shared prefixes) or share each fetch with more tokens (batching). Right of the ridge: you're paying for math, so you need a faster workbench or less math.

Cheat sheet

Idea One line
Roofline speed = min(math roof, memory roof × math per byte)
Ridge math roof ÷ memory roof. My CPU: 11. H100: ~295. B200: ~281
Memory-bound Left of the ridge. Typing, notebooks, small steps
Compute-bound Right of the ridge. Reading long questions, big batches
Batching Moves the table work right. Doesn't move the notebooks
Smaller numbers Fewer bytes, faster typing. The ridge stays put
Below the roof Software leaving speed on the table. Go look

What's next

The notebooks kept showing up as the job batching can't fix. Part 5: The KV Cache From Scratch builds the notebook by hand: what's in it, why it grows with every word, how big it gets for real models, and the tricks servers use to make it smaller.

Every number in this post comes from two scripts: roofline.py (measured on a 2-core cloud CPU with float32 NumPy) and predict.py (the one-line model applied to published chip specs). GPU figures are predictions from dense peak specs, not measurements, so treat them as ceilings.
aiSummary: 文章介绍了 Roofline 模型作为分析 LLM 推理性能的统一框架，展示了内存带宽和计算能力如何决定不同批次大小和操作下的速度上限。
oneSentenceSummary: 文章介绍了 Roofline 模型作为分析 LLM 推理性能的统一框架，展示了内存带宽和计算能力如何决定不同批次大小和操作下的速度上限。
summary: 文章解释了 Roofline 模型——一种性能分析工具，通过绘制内存带宽（叉车）和计算能力（工作台）来预测 LLM 推理速度。通过在 CPU 上的实证测量，文章展示了不同操作如何落在 Roofline 上：表格乘法随着批次大小增加而攀升斜率，笔记本读取保持内存受限，小型算术操作占据「地下室」区域。随后，该模型被应用于预测 8B 参数模型在 H100 GPU 上的性能，揭示单用户吞吐量受内存带宽限制（约 209 tokens/s），而批处理在达到脊点（约 295 tokens）之前提供免费吞吐量。分析最后给出了使用 Roofline 优化 LLM 服务的实用指南，通过识别工作负载是内存受限还是计算受限来进行优化。

mainPoints.point: Roofline 模型统一了 LLM 推理分析中的内存和计算瓶颈
mainPoints.explanation: 通过绘制内存带宽（斜屋顶）与计算能力（平屋顶）的关系，该模型识别出工作负载从内存受限过渡到计算受限的脊点，从而能够在实际执行前预测性能上限。

mainPoints.point: LLM 推理操作根据其算术强度在 Roofline 上呈现不同位置
mainPoints.explanation: 表格乘法随着批次大小增加而攀升斜率，笔记本读取在低算术强度（0.5 FLOPs/byte）下保持内存受限，小型算术操作占据地下室区域（0.08 FLOPs/byte），这解释了为什么内核融合和批处理是关键优化手段。

mainPoints.point: GPU 预测显示内存带宽仍是大多数 LLM 服务场景的主要瓶颈
mainPoints.explanation: 对于 8B 参数模型在 H100 上，单用户吞吐量因内存获取时间被限制在约 209 tokens/s，而批处理在计算成为限制之前，每批最多约 295 tokens 提供免费吞吐量，这表明量化（FP8）提高了单用户速度，但并未移动脊点。

keyQuotes: 工程师称之为 Roofline 模型，这是我所知的对于 LLM 推理最有用的草图。
速度 = （工作台速度）和（叉车速度 × 每字节数学运算量）中的较小者
在这个芯片上，这个模型下单个用户永远无法获得超过约 209 词/秒的速度。
更小的数字让单个用户输入速度翻倍。
